blocks.text: Derived (associated) lipids are the hydrolysis products of simple and compound lipids that keep the characteristics of lipids, for example fatty acids, glycerol, steroids, lipid-soluble vitamins and terpenes. They come from fats rather than being fats themselves, and they have important roles in energy and hormone production, cell structure, nerve health and vitamin function.

Steroids are not made from fatty acids but have some lipid-like properties. They contain three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring fused together, the steroid nucleus; the rings are labelled A, B, C and D. Many steroids also have an -OH group, which puts them in the alcohol class (sterols). There are many steroids in living systems, including cholesterol, bile salts, vitamin D and the steroid hormones.

blocks.alt: The steroid nucleus: three six-membered rings A, B and C and a five-membered ring D fused together, with a CH3 group at the A/B ring junction and at the C/D ring junction, and R on ring D.
blocks.caption: Figure 27.12: Steroid ring structure (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 27.12).

blocks.text: Plants contain a wide variety of hydrocarbons called terpenes, built from isoprene units. These hydrocarbons and their oxygen-containing derivatives have fewer than 40 carbon atoms; terpenes with 40 carbon atoms are called carotenoids. Limonene, found in lemons, is a terpene.

blocks.alt: Skeletal structure of limonene: a six-membered ring with one C=C double bond and a methyl group on the double-bond carbon; on the opposite ring carbon a hashed bond leads to a carbon bearing a methyl group and a =CH2 group. Labelled limonene (a terpene).
blocks.caption: Limonene (a terpene) (original drawing after the structure printed beside topic 27.4.4).
